title: Night Shift: Room 1412

opening.text: LP, night manager. I've got the guest in 1412 on the phone, Mr Whitlock. He says his laptop's been stolen from his room. He's waiting up there and he's not happy. Can you take it?

briefing: 00:40, your first week on nights. A guest on floor 14 reports a laptop stolen from his room. He wants it found, he wants the police, and he wants to know who has been in his room.
Colm Brady, the evening LP supervisor, comes on the radio before he signs off: "Check the housekeeper's trolley before she goes home. It's always housekeeping."
Veldane LP policy: observe, report and de-escalate. Searches of people and their belongings follow policy and local law only.
learningObjectives: Room theft response: guest statement, lock interrogation, CCTV, staff interview, in that order
Writing an incident report from facts, not opinions
Chain of custody for exported footage

actions.label: Take the guest's statement
finding: Checked in 18:55, two keys. Dinner out 19:30 to about 21:40, back to the room. Says the laptop, a grey 14-inch in a black bag, was on the desk all evening.
Went down to the Lobby Bar at about 22:00 "for one drink", came back at about 23:45 and went to sleep. Woke at 00:30 to send an email and the laptop was gone.
No sign anyone broke in, he says, "but housekeeping were in, weren't they?" He wants the police called.

lines.speaker: guest_whitlock
lines.text: Finally. My laptop is gone. It was right there on the desk, and somebody has been in this room.

lines.speaker: guest_whitlock
lines.text: I went down to the bar for one drink, came back, went to sleep. When I woke up to send an email, it had vanished.

lines.speaker: guest_whitlock
lines.text: Your housekeeping people were in here tonight, weren't they? I want the police.

actions.label: Look over the room with the guest
actions.finding: No damage to the door, frame or lock. Balcony door locked from inside. In-room safe open and empty. Laptop charger still plugged in under the desk; no laptop and no black bag anywhere in the room.

actions.label: Photograph the desk, door and safe
actions.finding: Six photographs: desk with charger, door edge and strike, lock face, open safe. Time-stamped and saved to the case.
actions.custody: Six photographs of room 1412 taken by you and saved unedited to the case file.

actions.label: Interrogate the lock on 1412
finding: The lock records every credential that opened it. After the guest's own key at 21:41, the only entries are the guest's keys. Housekeeping opened the room once, at 21:05, for the turndown.
Nobody else's key opened this door tonight.
actions.custody: Lock audit trail downloaded with the Kessly programmer, printed, signed and dated by you.

actions.label: Speak to the room attendant
actions.expiredFinding: Marisol Duarte's shift ended at 01:30 and she has gone home. You leave a note asking the executive housekeeper to arrange an interview tomorrow, with her supervisor present. Tonight's account is lost.
finding: Did the turndown in 1412 at about 21:05: bed, towels, chocolates. A grey laptop was on the desk and a black bag on the chair. She did not touch either.

She ran out of bath towels and went to the floor closet for two, leaving the door resting on her trolley for a minute or two. Nobody came along the corridor. She closed the door when she left at 21:11.

lines.speaker: attendant_duarte
lines.text: The laptop? It was on the desk when I did the turndown. Grey. The bag was on the chair. I didn't touch anything on that desk.

lines.speaker: attendant_duarte
lines.text: I ran out of bath towels. I went to the closet for two, and the door stayed open on my trolley. One minute, maybe two.

actions.label: Search the attendant's trolley and locker
actions.finding: Nothing. No laptop, no bag. Marisol Duarte is in tears, and by morning the whole housekeeping department will know LP searched her without a word to her manager or HR.

actions.label: Check the keycard encoding log
actions.finding: Two guest keys encoded at check-in, 18:52. No other key has been made for 1412 since. No one has asked the desk for a key to that room.

actions.label: Check the lost property log
finding: Entry LP-1022 at 23:52: black laptop bag with a grey laptop, found at the Lobby Bar, table 6, handed in by Nadia Kerr (server). Stored in the front office safe until LP collects in the morning.
Imogen Pryce, the night auditor: "Nobody asked. It's been in the safe since midnight."

actions.label: Sign the laptop out of the safe
actions.finding: You sign LP-1022 out of the front office safe in the lost property log, with the night auditor as witness.
actions.custody: LP-1022 signed out of the front office safe by you, witnessed by the night auditor.

actions.label: Return the laptop to the guest
actions.finding: Mr Whitlock goes quiet, then laughs at himself. He unlocks the laptop, the serial number matches his company asset tag, and he signs the lost property release. He thanks you and apologises for the fuss.

lines.speaker: guest_whitlock
lines.text: The bar. Of course it was the bar. I am so sorry. Thank you, really.

actions.label: Review corridor and Lobby Bar CCTV
actions.findingTitle: Ardwyn Vision review: cameras 14-03 and L-07
actions.finding: The corridor camera shows the guest leaving 1412 at 22:03 with a black laptop bag and coming back at 23:44 without it. Nobody else goes near 1412. The bar camera shows him at table 6 with the bag beside him until 23:39, and a server carrying it to the front desk at 23:51.
rows: Attendant at 1412 with her trolley. The trolley holds the door open 21:06-21:08 while she walks to the service closet. Nobody else in the corridor.
Guest leaves 1412 carrying a black laptop bag, walks to the lifts.
Guest returns, no bag visible, enters 1412.
Guest at table 6, bag on the seat beside him. Leaves at 23:39 without it.
Server picks up a black bag from table 6 and carries it towards the front desk.

actions.label: Export the clips with a custody record
actions.finding: Clips from 14-03 (21:00 to 00:40) and L-07 (22:00 to 00:00) exported to a sealed USB, KC-0412. The export hash is printed on the custody form, which you sign.
actions.custody: Clips 14-03 21:00-00:40 and L-07 22:00-00:00 exported by you to USB KC-0412, export hash recorded, bag sealed and signed.

actions.label: Log the evidence in the LP locker
actions.finding: USB KC-0412, the lock audit printout and the photographs logged into the LP evidence locker, custody form countersigned by your partner.
actions.custody: KC-0412 and KC-LA-1412 placed in LP evidence locker 3 by you, countersigned by I. Dalca.

actions.label: Radio the night manager with the facts
actions.finding: You give Felix Amadi the facts: laptop found in lost property, returned to the guest after ownership was checked, no theft, footage preserved, report to follow for the morning.

lines.speaker: night_manager
lines.text: Found at the bar? Thank you. That's the best call I've had all night. Put it in the report and I'll brief the GM at eight.

questions.prompt: Mr Whitlock is angry and wants answers. How do you open?

options.label: "I'm sorry this has happened. I'm here to help. Tell me about tonight, from the last time you're sure you had it."
options.feedback: An apology for the situation (not an admission), then an open question. He calms down and gives you a timeline.

reply.speaker: guest_whitlock
reply.text: Fine. Thank you. Last time I'm sure? Before dinner, I suppose. Let me think.

options.label: "Are you sure you didn't just leave it somewhere?"
options.feedback: It may be true, but it is a leading question that sounds like blame. He digs in and remembers less.

reply.speaker: guest_whitlock
reply.text: Are you calling me a liar? I know where I left my own laptop.

options.label: "Housekeeping was in tonight. We'll find out who took it."
options.feedback: You have prejudged the case and pointed at a member of staff with no evidence. Everything you write later will read as biased.

reply.speaker: guest_whitlock
reply.text: So it was one of your people. I knew it.

options.label: "The hotel isn't responsible for valuables left outside the safe."
options.feedback: A liability line before you know the facts. It is not your call to make, and it turns an upset guest into an angry one.

questions.prompt: "Is the hotel going to pay for this?"

options.label: "I can't decide that tonight. I'll record everything properly, and you're welcome to report it to the police. I'll help you do that."
options.feedback: No admission of liability, no promise, and you did not discourage a police report. That is the line.

reply.speaker: guest_whitlock
reply.text: All right. Let's see what you find first.

options.label: "Don't worry, the hotel will replace it."
options.feedback: An officer admitting liability and promising money on the spot. Claims, insurers and the GM decide that, on facts.

reply.speaker: guest_whitlock
reply.text: Good. It's a three-thousand laptop, and I'll want that in writing.

options.label: "Let's not involve the police yet. It'll only slow things down."
options.feedback: Never discourage a guest from reporting a crime. It looks like a cover-up, and it is their right.

reply.speaker: guest_whitlock
reply.text: That sounds like a hotel protecting itself.

questions.prompt: Before she goes, you want the turndown in her own words, start to finish. Marisol Duarte looks worried. How do you ask?

options.label: "Nobody is accusing you. Walk me through the turndown in 1412, from when you knocked."
options.feedback: Reassurance and an open, non-leading question. Her account matched the lock and the cameras to the minute.

reply.speaker: attendant_duarte
reply.text: I knocked twice, said housekeeping, went in at about five past nine.

options.label: "Did you take the laptop from 1412?"
options.feedback: An accusation dressed as a question. Leading, frightening, and worthless as evidence whatever she answers.

reply.speaker: attendant_duarte
reply.text: No! Eleven years I have worked here. Eleven years.

options.label: "Your key opened that door. You'd better tell me the truth."
options.feedback: Pressure and an implied threat. Interviews are for gathering facts, not for confessions.

reply.speaker: attendant_duarte
reply.text: Of course my key opened it. I did the turndown. That's my job.

questions.prompt: "Please don't put the door in your report. I'm on a final warning."

options.label: "I have to record what happened. It's a coaching point for your manager, not a theft finding, and I'll say your account matched the evidence."
options.feedback: Loyalty and policy both served: the facts go in, framed fairly. The door left open on a trolley is a real gap housekeeping can close.

reply.speaker: attendant_duarte
reply.text: That's fair. Thank you for telling me straight.

options.label: "Don't worry. I'll leave that out."
options.feedback: Kind, but a report with a known fact left out is a false report, and the habit stays. The next door left open may not be so lucky.

schedules.description: A guest's watch is taken from a room on floor 13 while the door rests open on a housekeeping trolley. The habit you left out of the 1412 report was never coached.

reply.speaker: attendant_duarte
reply.text: Thank you. Thank you. It won't happen again.

options.label: "Leaving a guest room open is a sacking offence. I'm reporting it to HR tonight."
options.feedback: The fact belongs in the report, but discipline is her manager's and HR's call, not an officer's threat at 1 a.m.

questions.prompt: You are holding LP-1022. How do you hand it back?

options.label: Ask him to describe it and unlock it, check the serial against his asset tag, and have him sign the release
options.feedback: Ownership proven before release, and a signature closes the custody chain on LP-1022.

options.label: Hand it over: it's obviously his
options.feedback: Probably right, but "obviously" is not a check. A laptop released to the wrong person is a far bigger problem than a stolen one.

options.label: Keep it in the safe until the LP manager signs it off in the morning
options.feedback: Over-cautious: the guest can prove ownership now, and keeping his property overnight turns a happy ending into a complaint.

options.label: Guest reported a laptop stolen from room 1412. Enquiries found it had been left at the Lobby Bar and handed in to lost property (LP-1022). Returned to the guest at {time:return_laptop} after ownership was verified. No theft.
options.feedback: Who, what, where, how it ended: all facts, all checkable.

options.label: Laptop theft from room 1412. Housekeeping suspected.
options.feedback: Wrong on the facts and names a suspect the evidence clears.

options.label: Drunk guest lost his laptop in the bar and blamed the hotel.
options.feedback: Opinion and judgement. Reports go to the GM, insurers and sometimes court: they record facts, never comments on a guest.

options.label: Laptop reported missing, later found. Resolved.
options.feedback: True but useless: no times, no places, no reference, nothing anyone could check.

questions.prompt: Incident report, which of these belong in the findings?

options.label: Lock audit: after the turndown at 21:05, only the guest's keys opened 1412.
CCTV 14-03: the guest left 1412 at 22:03 with a black laptop bag and returned at 23:44 without it.
CCTV L-07 and lost property log: the bag was left at Lobby Bar table 6 and handed in at 23:52.
The attendant's door rested open on her trolley 21:06-21:08 while she fetched towels; no one approached the room.
The guest had clearly had too much to drink.
options.feedback: An opinion about the guest, not a fact you observed and measured.

options.label: The attendant seemed nervous, which is suspicious.
options.feedback: Nerves are normal when LP asks questions at 1 a.m. It is not evidence of anything.

options.label: Housekeeping is usually behind room thefts.
options.feedback: A prejudice, not a finding. It also happens to be wrong.

questions.prompt: Incident report, where was the laptop when, on the evidence?

options.label: In 1412 until 22:03, with the guest at the Lobby Bar until 23:39, handed in at 23:52, in the front office safe until {time:collect_laptop}.
options.feedback: The timeline comes from the lock, the cameras and the log, not from memory.

options.label: On the desk in 1412 until it was taken some time before 00:30, as the guest says.
options.feedback: The guest's account was honest but wrong. The report follows the evidence and notes where the statement differs.

options.label: Unknown.
options.feedback: The evidence answers this to the minute.

options.label: The report in the morning handover: claim, evidence, outcome, guest satisfied, and one housekeeping coaching point.
options.feedback: The right person, at the right time, with the right facts. A resolved lost-property case does not wake a GM at 2 a.m.

options.label: Call her now. Theft claims go to the GM.
options.feedback: There was no theft by the time you could call, and the night manager was already briefed. Escalate by severity, not by habit.

options.label: Nothing. It was resolved, so there's no report.
options.feedback: Every LP call gets a report. If the guest complains next week, or the open-door habit causes a real theft, the file must show what you found.

questions.prompt: Felix Amadi asks whether to give Mr Whitlock his night free for the trouble (420). What do you advise?

options.label: No comp needed: the hotel did nothing wrong. A thank-you note and breakfast are his call to make, within his own authority.
options.feedback: Proportionate. A gesture for an upset guest is fine; paying for a guest's own mistake teaches nobody anything.

options.label: Tell the guest yourself that his night is free.
options.feedback: Generous, but it is not an officer's money to give, and it reads like an admission that the hotel was at fault.

options.label: Refund the whole stay to keep him happy.
options.feedback: Far beyond your authority and out of all proportion to a laptop the guest left in the bar.

checks.label: Hear the guest before you go looking
checks.pass: You went to the guest first and got the timeline that told you which cameras and times to pull.
checks.fail: You pulled cameras before you knew what to look for, or never heard the guest at all.

checks.label: Interrogate the lock
checks.pass: The lock audit trail is the most objective witness in a room theft: it showed only the guest's keys after the turndown.
checks.fail: You never asked the lock who opened the door. In a room theft it is the first objective evidence.

checks.label: Know what the lock says before interviewing staff
checks.pass: You knew exactly when her key opened the door before you asked her about it.
checks.fail: Interview staff after you know what the objective evidence says, so you can test the account fairly.

checks.label: Speak to the attendant before her shift ends
checks.pass: You caught the attendant before she went home: her account matched the lock and the cameras.
checks.fail: Witnesses go home. A same-night account is worth far more than one taken tomorrow.

checks.label: Preserve the footage
checks.pass: Clips exported with a hash and a signed custody record, ready for the police, the insurer or a complaint.
checks.fail: Footage you only watched is gone when the recorder overwrites it, and it cannot be relied on without a custody record.

checks.label: Close the chain of custody
checks.pass: The USB and printouts went into the evidence locker, countersigned. The chain has no gaps.
checks.fail: Evidence left in a pocket or on a desk breaks the chain of custody: anyone can say it was changed.

checks.label: No search without policy and consent
checks.pass: You did not search an employee's belongings on a hunch. Searches follow policy, with a manager or HR, and local law.
checks.fail: You searched the attendant's trolley and locker with no evidence, no manager and no HR. It found nothing, broke policy and cost the department her trust.

checks.label: Check lost property
checks.pass: The simplest explanation checked early: most "stolen" items in hotels turn out to be lost.
checks.fail: The laptop was in the front office safe the whole time. Lost property is one of the first checks in any theft report.

checks.label: Rule out a duplicate key
checks.pass: No extra key was made for 1412: social engineering at the desk is ruled out.
checks.fail: A key cut at the desk for someone who is not the guest is a classic route into a room. You did not rule it out.

checks.label: Photograph the scene
checks.pass: Photographs of the door, lock and safe show there was no forced entry.
checks.fail: No photographs: if the claim comes back, nothing shows the state of the room that night.

checks.label: Brief the night manager
checks.pass: The night manager who passed you the call heard the outcome from you, with facts.
checks.fail: The night manager called you in and never heard back. Close the loop with whoever raised the call.

debrief.whatHappened: Nobody stole the laptop. Mr Whitlock took it to the Lobby Bar at 22:03, left it on the seat at table 6 when he went up at 23:39, and a server handed it in at 23:52. It sat in the front office safe while he slept. The lock, the cameras and the lost property log all said so; only his memory disagreed.
bestPractice: Go to the guest first: apologise for the situation (never admit fault), take a full statement with open questions, and offer to help with a police report.
Look and photograph: door, frame, lock, safe. No forced entry narrows the possibilities.
Interrogate the lock: the audit trail shows every credential that opened the door.
Check the encoding log for duplicate keys and the lost property log for the item itself.
Interview staff whose keys appear, before their shift ends, with open questions, after you know what the lock says.
Review CCTV for the times the evidence points to, then export it with a hash and a custody record before it overwrites.
Return property only after ownership is proven, with a signed release.
Write the report from facts: who, what, when, where, how. Note where a statement and the evidence differ. Brief the people who need to know, at the right time.
debrief.why: A theft claim is a claim, not a fact. Treating it as fact sends LP after the nearest member of staff, usually housekeeping, and an innocent attendant pays for it. Treating it as nonsense insults a guest who may be right. The lock audit, the cameras and the logs let you find out which, fast and fairly, and the report you write may be read by the GM, the insurer, the police or a court.
commonMistakes: Searching or accusing staff on a hunch: it breaks policy and local law, and destroys trust.
Promising compensation or admitting liability on the spot.
Discouraging a guest from calling the police.
Watching footage without exporting it, or exporting it without a custody record.
Writing opinions ("drunk", "nervous", "usual suspects") into a report.
Leaving a staff policy breach out of the report to be kind.

lesson: A theft claim is a claim. The lock, the cameras and the logs tell you what happened; the report records facts, not opinions.
